content: I feel like I can't shake this idea that everything that happened was my fault. Even though everyone says it wasn’t personal, I just can’t believe them. It’s like a constant echo in my head telling me I’m not good enough. And every time someone tries to explain it away as part of the company's restructuring, I still hear their voices saying “but why did they choose her?” It doesn't make sense to me how something so big and impersonal can feel so personal at the same time.
That must be really tough to carry around. Do you find there are certain moments or situations where it feels even stronger?

Yeah, it’s like every time I see a news article about layoffs or hear people talking about company changes, it just hits me harder. Even when I’m out with friends and they talk about their jobs, I feel this knot in my stomach because I know what could happen. It's like the fear is always there, waiting to remind me that I'm not good enough for any of it. And then sometimes, even when I try to distract myself or do something fun, these thoughts just come back and ruin everything.
It sounds exhausting to have those thoughts pop up so frequently. Do you find anything helps calm the knot in your stomach even a little bit?

I don’t know if there’s really anything that helps. Sometimes I try to distract myself with movies or books, but it doesn't last long before my mind starts wandering back to all of this. It's like no matter what I do, these feelings are just always there under the surface, ready to come up and make me feel bad again. Even when people try to be supportive and tell me it’s not my fault, a part of me still doubts them and thinks they’re just being nice or that they don’t really understand how I’m feeling inside.
It sounds like you're doing your best to cope with those feelings. Have there been times when talking about these thoughts with someone close to you has helped, even if only a little?

Sometimes it does help to talk about it, but mostly because they try to listen and understand what I’m going through. But then again, no matter how much they say they get it, there’s still this part of me that feels like they can’t possibly know how deep down I feel responsible for everything. It’s frustrating because even when people are trying to help, I end up feeling more alone because nothing seems to change the way I see myself.
It sounds challenging to balance those moments of connection with the lingering feelings of doubt. Do you ever find a particular person or type of conversation that feels especially supportive?

There are times when talking to my sister helps, but even then, it’s hard because she can’t really fix how I feel inside. She tries her best to reassure me and tells me it wasn’t my fault, but deep down, I still struggle with believing her. It’s like no matter what anyone says, there’s this voice in my head that keeps whispering that I’m the reason everything fell apart. And when she leaves or we finish talking, those doubts come rushing back, making me feel even more isolated and unsure of myself.

It sounds tough to have those doubts persist even after talking with someone close like your sister. Do you ever do something specific right after these conversations that helps ease the return of those feelings?

After talking to my sister or anyone else, I usually end up feeling a bit better for a moment, but then it all comes flooding back pretty quickly. Sometimes I try to write down what they said or even make notes about why they think it wasn’t my fault, hoping that seeing it on paper might help me believe it more. But honestly, the words just don't stick in my head like my own doubts do. It’s frustrating because I want so badly to feel better and trust that others are right, but the self-blame is too strong.
Writing things down can be a good way to try and hold onto those supportive thoughts. Do you find any other activities help keep those positive feelings around longer?

I’ve tried different things like writing or even journaling about what happened, but it doesn’t seem to make much of a difference in the long run. It’s like no matter how many times I tell myself it wasn’t my fault, that voice inside me is louder and more persistent. Sometimes I try to go for walks or do something relaxing, hoping it will help clear my head, but those feelings always creep back in. It’s exhausting because even when I’m trying to be positive, there’s this constant nagging doubt that ruins everything.
It sounds really draining to have those doubts persist so strongly. Do you find any particular activities or moments where you feel a bit more at peace, even if just for a short while?

There are rare moments when I do feel a little better, usually right after talking with someone who listens and tries to reassure me. For example, my sister sometimes shares stories about how others have faced similar situations and came out okay, which can be comforting in the moment. But as soon as we hang up or move on from that conversation, the doubts start creeping back.

Sometimes, when I’m alone, if I manage to distract myself with a good book or a movie, there are brief moments where I forget about everything for a little while. It’s like a temporary escape, but it doesn’t last long and the feelings always come rushing back once I stop whatever I was doing. It’s frustrating because even those small moments of peace feel so fleeting and unreliable.
Those moments of distraction with books or movies can be nice escapes. Do you have any plans for what you might do next to try and find a bit more lasting comfort?

I don’t really know what to do next, honestly. It feels like no matter what I try, the self-blame just keeps coming back stronger than before. Sometimes I think about looking for another job or trying to figure out my next steps, but even thinking about that makes me feel anxious and inadequate. It’s hard because part of me wants to move forward and prove myself, but another part is too scared and doubtful to take any action.

I keep hoping that eventually, things will just get better on their own, but it feels like I’m stuck in this endless loop of negative thoughts. Even when people suggest different ways to cope or offer support, I end up feeling overwhelmed and unsure if anything will truly help. It’s a constant struggle, and right now, it seems easier to just stay where I am rather than face the fear of failing again.

It sounds like you’re in a tough spot with a lot on your mind. Taking small steps can sometimes feel manageable even when big changes seem daunting. Have you thought about what one small thing might look like for you right now?

I’ve thought about it, but the idea of taking any kind of step feels overwhelming. Even something as simple as updating my resume or reaching out to a friend seems too much to handle. It’s like every little task turns into this huge mountain that I’m sure I’ll never be able to climb. The thought of facing those tasks just reinforces how inadequate and incapable I feel.

I know people mean well when they suggest small steps, but it’s hard to see past the immediate fear and doubt. Right now, even thinking about taking a tiny step forward feels like admitting that I’m not okay with where I am, which is terrifying in itself. It’s a cycle of feeling stuck and then feeling worse because I can’t seem to break free from it.

It definitely sounds challenging to navigate those feelings. Sometimes just acknowledging the fear can be a step forward. Have you found any small moments or tasks that, even if they feel scary, might offer a tiny bit of relief or accomplishment?

Even thinking about small tasks feels daunting because every little thing seems like an insurmountable challenge right now. I know people mean well when they suggest taking baby steps, but it’s hard to see past the immediate fear and doubt. For example, updating my resume sounds so simple, but just the thought of doing it makes me feel anxious and overwhelmed.

I’ve tried a few times to reach out to friends or even start looking for job openings online, but as soon as I do, those doubts come flooding back, telling me that nothing will work out. It’s like no matter what small thing I try, my mind immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario, making it impossible to feel any sense of accomplishment.

Sometimes just acknowledging how scared and unsure I am feels exhausting. It’s a constant battle with these negative thoughts, and even when I try to take tiny steps, they end up reinforcing how much I fear failure.

It sounds really tough to navigate those immediate fears. Have you found any small moments or tasks that, even if brief, give you a sense of accomplishment or relief? Even the smallest wins can sometimes feel significant.

I’ve tried a few things here and there, but nothing seems to stick or provide lasting relief. For instance, I might force myself to send out one job application just to get it over with, but as soon as I hit "send," those doubts come rushing back. It’s like no matter how small the task, my mind immediately starts questioning everything.

Even when I manage to do something, like sending that email or updating a part of my resume, the sense of accomplishment is fleeting. As soon as I finish, I start worrying about whether it was good enough or if anyone will even respond. It’s frustrating because those small wins should feel better, but they just lead to more anxiety and self-doubt.

Sometimes, when I’m out for a walk or doing something relaxing like reading, there are brief moments where I forget about everything, but as soon as I stop, the doubts return full force. It feels like no matter what I do, those negative thoughts always come back stronger than before.

It sounds really challenging to have those fleeting moments of relief followed by strong doubts. Do you find any activities help you stay in that calm state a bit longer, even if it’s just for a short while?

Sometimes when I’m out walking or listening to music, I can get into a rhythm where my mind quiets down and the doubts fade away temporarily. It’s like being immersed in something else helps me escape those negative thoughts for a little bit. But as soon as I stop moving or the song ends, everything comes rushing back.

Even when I’m able to find that brief respite, it feels so fragile. The moment I start thinking about going home or returning to my usual routine, those doubts and fears come flooding in again. It’s frustrating because I know these moments are important for my mental well-being, but they’re so fleeting that it doesn’t feel like much of a solution.

It’s hard to stay in that calm state when everything else feels so overwhelming. Even the smallest disruptions can trigger those thoughts, making it difficult to maintain any sense of peace or relief.
Those moments of calm while walking or listening to music sound valuable even if they are brief. Do you have any plans for how you might incorporate more of these activities into your routine?

I’ve thought about trying to make those calming activities a regular part of my day, but the idea of sticking to a routine feels daunting. I know that walking or listening to music helps in the moment, but setting aside time for it consistently seems impossible right now.

Even planning to do something simple like going for a walk every afternoon makes me anxious because I worry about not being able to stick with it. The thought of failing at even small things just reinforces my feelings of inadequacy and fear. It’s hard to see how adding these activities could help when the doubts are so persistent.

I want to find ways to feel better, but every time I try to think about a plan or routine, those negative thoughts take over. Right now, it feels easier to just avoid thinking about it altogether rather than face the fear of not being able to follow through.

It sounds tough to navigate those fears while trying to set up a routine. Have you considered starting with very small, flexible goals that are less overwhelming? Maybe something as simple as going for a short walk whenever you feel like it, without pressure to do it at a specific time each day?

The idea of setting small, flexible goals sounds good in theory, but the thought of even trying feels overwhelming. I worry that if I start with something so small and flexible, I’ll end up not doing anything at all because I won’t feel like I’m making real progress.

Even thinking about going for a short walk whenever I feel like it makes me anxious because there’s this fear that I won’t actually do it. It’s hard to trust myself to follow through with even the smallest tasks when my mind is so consumed by doubts and fears. The pressure of trying to stick to anything, no matter how small or flexible, just adds another layer of stress.

Right now, it feels safer to avoid setting any goals at all rather than risk failing at them. It’s a cycle where I want to do better but the fear of not being able to follow through keeps me from even starting.

It sounds like finding that balance between wanting to improve and managing those fears is tough. Have you thought about just noticing when you feel like going for a walk, without putting pressure on yourself to actually do it? Just observing those moments might be a step forward.

Noticing when I feel like going for a walk does sound less overwhelming than forcing myself to do something specific. But even that feels tricky because as soon as I notice the thought, my mind starts questioning whether I’ll actually follow through or if it’s just another fleeting moment.

It’s hard to separate the desire to take care of myself from the fear of not being able to act on it. Even observing those moments without pressure makes me anxious because there’s this worry that I won’t be able to notice them consistently. It feels like no matter what I try, my mind is always ready to doubt and criticize.

Right now, just acknowledging when I feel like going for a walk seems like a small step, but it still feels daunting. The fear of failure or not following through looms so large that even the smallest observation feels overwhelming.

It sounds like you’re being very mindful of those moments already. Maybe starting with simply noting them without judgment could be helpful. Even if it’s just for a moment, acknowledging the desire can be a step forward.

Do you find any comfort in knowing you’ve noticed that feeling to go for a walk, even if you don’t act on it right away?

Noticing the feeling to go for a walk without judgment does sound simpler, but even that feels hard. When I do notice the desire, there’s this immediate doubt about whether I’ll actually follow through or if it was just another fleeting thought. It’s like my mind is always questioning and doubting every little thing.

Even though acknowledging the feeling seems small, it still triggers a lot of anxiety because I worry that I won’t be able to do anything with it. The fear of not being able to act on those moments feels so strong that even noticing them without judgment doesn’t feel like much of a relief.

Right now, just trying to notice these fleeting desires feels overwhelming because they’re quickly overshadowed by doubts and fears about failing to follow through. It’s a constant struggle between wanting to take care of myself and the fear of not being able to do it.

It sounds really challenging to navigate those immediate doubts. Noticing them without judgment can be a step, even if small. Do you find any comfort in acknowledging these moments, even briefly? Sometimes just recognizing what’s happening can feel like a tiny victory.

Acknowledging the moment when I feel like going for a walk does offer some brief relief, but it’s fleeting and quickly overshadowed by doubts. It feels good to recognize that desire, but as soon as I do, my mind starts questioning whether I’ll actually go through with it or if it was just another passing thought.

Even though it’s small, noticing those moments without judgment can be a tiny victory, but the fear of not following through is so strong that it quickly takes over. It’s like every time I notice something positive, there’s an immediate counterbalance of doubt and anxiety.

Right now, even these brief moments of recognition feel fragile because they’re so easily disrupted by my fears. It’s frustrating because I know acknowledging them could be helpful, but the doubts are just too persistent to let it stick.

It sounds like those fleeting moments of recognition can still offer a bit of relief, even if brief. Noticing them without judgment is indeed a small victory. Do you find any comfort in these tiny victories, no matter how fleeting they may be?

Those tiny victories do offer some comfort, but it’s hard to hold onto that feeling for long. When I notice the desire to go for a walk and acknowledge it without judgment, there is a brief sense of relief. It feels good in the moment, but as soon as I start thinking about actually going or not following through, those doubts come rushing back.

Even though these small moments are fleeting, they do provide a tiny bit of peace that can be comforting. Recognizing them helps me see that there are times when I’m capable of noticing something positive, even if it’s just for a moment. But the fear and doubt always seem to catch up quickly, making it difficult to sustain any sense of accomplishment or relief.

It’s frustrating because I know these small victories could be more helpful if they lasted longer, but my mind is so quick to undermine them that it feels like an uphill battle.

It sounds like those fleeting moments of recognition are still valuable, even if brief. Noticing them can be a step forward, and holding onto the comfort they bring, no matter how short-lived, might help over time. Do you find any particular thoughts or feelings more comforting than others during these moments?

During those fleeting moments when I notice something positive, like feeling the desire to go for a walk, there is a sense of clarity and peace that feels comforting. It’s a brief respite from the constant doubts and fears. In those moments, it feels like my mind isn’t cluttered with negative thoughts, and I can see things more clearly.

However, even these small moments are quickly overshadowed by the fear of not being able to follow through or the worry that the doubts will return. It’s hard to hold onto that sense of clarity because as soon as I start thinking about what might happen next, those doubts come back stronger than before.

Despite this, acknowledging and holding onto those brief moments of comfort can be a small step forward. Even if it only lasts for a moment, recognizing the positive feeling helps me see that there are times when I’m not entirely consumed by negative thoughts. It’s a fragile comfort, but it does offer some relief in an otherwise overwhelming situation.
